segments.title: Mikasa's guns and bilingual museum displays
segments.summary: Mikasa's deck, six-inch gun, and bilingual displays show how the preserved ship presents its history to visitors.
segments.body: This update opens on Mikasa's deck beside one of the ship's six-inch guns. Displays in English and Japanese explain the vessel's history. The preserved warship provides a physical setting for those exhibits, allowing the gun and the historical account to be examined together. The museum is recommended as a rewarding place to explore.

evidence.note: The transcript recommends the ship, notes its six-inch gun, and describes English and Japanese historical displays.

segments.title: Different paths to naval hero status
segments.summary: A museum display places John Paul Jones beside Horatio Nelson and a third admiral, prompting a comparison between guerrilla-style service and more conventional fleet action and cruising.
segments.body: The display groups Horatio Nelson, John Paul Jones, and a third admiral whose name is unclear in the transcript. Their national standing is described as comparable, although their operational careers were very different. Jones is characterized as a guerrilla-warfare officer, while the other two are associated with traditional fleet action and cruising. The comparison does not rank one above the others; it asks what each officer did well and what kinds of naval service made them famous. This is a useful point for studying naval leadership through operational experience rather than treating national hero status as one uniform category.

evidence.note: The transcript compares a display including Nelson and John Paul Jones, contrasting Jones's guerrilla-style role with fleet action and cruising officers.
